第 81 章 Taking On Inclusion承担包容

Jason Wong / 杰森·黄

— 第 223 页 —

So, you're a leader of a 5- to 30-person engineering organization. You've heard of all the benefits of diversity. You believe it's the right thing to do for your business and for society. And, you now find yourself sitting around a table with your all-male leadership team wondering how you can hire more underrepresented minorities. First, congratulations for thinking about this now. There will be no easier time to fix your diversity problems than today. The good news is that finding diverse candidates is literally the easiest problem to solve. The bad news is that you're thinking about the wrong problem.

你是一个 5 到 30 人工程组织的领导。你听说过多元化的所有好处。你相信这对你的业务和社会是正确的事。现在你发现自己和全男性的领导团队围坐在桌旁，想知道怎么招更多代表性不足的少数族裔。首先，恭喜你现在就开始想这件事。没有比今天更容易解决多元化问题的时候了。好消息是找多元化候选人简直是最容易解决的问题。坏消息是你在想错误的问题。

I've talked with enough leaders of small companies to know there's a lack of understanding of what supporting diversity truly means and how much effort it requires. Most leaders start their efforts by focusing on where to find and how to hire underrepresented minorities. But, assuming your company allows these folks to make it through the door, what happens next? The answer: terrible things. Having been through transforming an almost all-male engineering team into a diverse organization, I can tell you that our workplaces are meat grinders. By default, they are wildly unsafe places for underrepresented minorities (URMs). URMs on average get paid less than their white male counterparts, are promoted less frequently, and experience high degrees of harassment. If you're lucky, it comes in the form of casual jokes or comments. If you're like most, there are far more serious acts being committed. And, to truly reap the benefits of diversity, you're going to need to address these issues head on.

我和足够多的小公司领导谈过，知道他们缺乏对支持多元化真正意味着什么、需要多少努力的理解。大多数领导从聚焦在哪里找和怎么招代表性不足少数族裔开始努力。但是，假设你的公司让这些人通过了门，接下来发生什么？答案：糟糕的事情。经历过把一个几乎全男性的工程团队转变为多元化组织，我可以告诉你我们的工作场所是绞肉机。默认情况下，它们对代表性不足少数族裔 (URM) 极其不安全。URM 平均比白人男性同行薪资低、晋升不频繁、经历高度骚扰。如果你幸运，它以随意的玩笑或评论形式出现。如果你和大多数人一样，有严重得多的行为在发生。而且，要真正收获多元化的好处，你需要正面解决这些问题。

— 第 224 页 —

When I prepare engineering leaders for this work, I talk about three inflection points that I've found to be common stumbling points. The first is not complicit to complicit. We all like to think of ourselves as good people. Or, at least inert enough to not be actively causing harm to others. So being called out for perpetuating sexism and discrimination is really tough to take in. What's important to recognize is that the forces that lead to our biases are systemic. We are all complicit in some way, even the most fervent supporters of diversity and inclusion. And, similar to the stages of grief, getting to acceptance is key to moving forward. So, the question isn't whether we are complicit, but how complicit are we and what are we going to do now that we're aware?

当我让工程领导为这项工作做准备时，我谈三个我发现是常见绊脚石的拐点。第一个是从不共谋到共谋。我们都喜欢把自己想成好人。或者至少足够惰性不主动伤害别人。所以因为延续性别歧视和歧视被指出是很难接受的。重要的是认识到导致我们偏见的力量是系统性的。我们都在某种程度上是共谋者，即使是多元化和包容最热情的支持者。而且，类似悲伤的阶段，达到接受是前进的关键。所以问题不是我们是否共谋，而是我们多共谋、既然意识到了我们打算做什么。

The second inflection point is believing in the lived experiences of others. After we open ourselves up to hearing from different voices, the next phase is actually believing what we're hearing. Because we live in a world filled with bias, two people can do the exact same thing and end up with very different outcomes. Marginalized people who report discrimination often find that doing so negatively affects their careers. When URMs raise issues, they often are labeled complainers or trouble-makers, whereas those they complain about have historically seen no consequences or repercussions for their actions. Defaulting to believing the lived experiences of others ensures you can expose and address the issues of inequity in your workplace.

第二个拐点是相信别人的生活体验。在我们开放自己倾听不同声音后，下一阶段是真正相信我们听到的。因为我们生活在一个充满偏见的世界，两个人做完全一样的事最终可能得到非常不同的结果。报告歧视的边缘化人群经常发现这样做对他们的职业生涯有负面影响。当 URM 提出问题时，他们经常被贴上抱怨者或麻烦制造者的标签，而他们抱怨的人历史上对行为没看到后果或反响。默认相信别人的生活体验确保你能揭露和解决工作场所的不公问题。

Finally, spending time and money. Talk is cheap. When someone comes to you and asks for $25,000 for an employee resource group program or to divert engineering for the next week to remove master/slave terminology from your codebase, you will hesitate. And the question is this: will you actually follow through? The thing about these inflection points is that you will encounter them over and over again. You will accept one aspect of your complicitness and then come across another. You will begin to believe one set of lived experiences while still being incredulous of someone else's. You will hear how your words and actions (or inactions!) are contributing to the problem and not the solution. You will not believe people when they tell you this. You will need to accept that they are probably right. This work is difficult. And tiring. And frustrating. But if you're successful, not only will your business be far more likely to succeed, but you will have created a new norm—one in which all identities are welcome and where equitable treatment and fair outcomes prevail.

最后，花时间和钱。谈话很便宜。当有人来找你要 25000 美元做员工资源组项目，或者下周把工程转去从代码库中移除 master/slave 术语时，你会犹豫。问题是：你真的会跟进吗？这些拐点的事情是你会一次又一次遇到。你会接受你共谋的一个方面然后遇到另一个。你会开始相信一套生活体验同时仍然怀疑别人的。你会听到你的言行（或无为！）怎么在促成问题而不是解决方案。人们告诉你这个时你不会相信。你需要接受他们可能是对的。这项工作困难。累人。令人沮丧。但如果你成功了，不仅你的业务更可能成功，而且你将创造一个新常态——一个所有身份都受欢迎、公平对待和公平结果占上风的新常态。
